Sortition could reduce this dependence because randomly selected citizens would not need to:

  • Raise campaign funds
  • Appease donors

Elections give citizens periodic opportunities to choose among candidates, but most people do not directly participate in lawmaking. Under sortition, ordinary people could exercise political authority themselves rather than merely selecting professional representatives.

This might produce a more participatory form of democracy in which citizens:

  • Deliberate over actual legislation
  • Hear evidence from experts and affected groups
  • Negotiate compromises
  • Experience the practical difficulty of governing
  • Develop greater civic knowledge and political confidence

Service could also make government feel less like a separate political class and more like a shared civic responsibility.

4. Encouraging deliberation rather than political competition

Elections reward messages that are simple, emotionally compelling, and easy to communicate. Candidates may benefit from polarization, negative campaigning, and appeals to highly motivated partisan groups.

A randomly selected body would not have to win votes or constantly attract media attention. If members received balanced briefings, expert testimony, and time for discussion, they might be more willing to:

  • Consider evidence that conflicts with their initial views
  • Change their positions
  • Seek compromise
  • Address long-term problems
  • Examine unpopular but necessary policies

Sortition advocates therefore argue that it could replace some of the incentives of electoral politics—competition, branding, fundraising, and partisan mobilization—with incentives for collective reasoning.

5. Weakening entrenched political parties

In an electoral system, parties often control nominations, campaign resources, legislative agendas, and political careers. This can narrow the range of candidates and policies available to voters.

Sortition could make parties less dominant because officeholders would not owe their positions to party organizations. Legislators could be selected independently of party labels, allowing more varied viewpoints and reducing automatic party-line voting.

This might also make it harder for a small group of professional politicians to control government over decades.

6. Lowering barriers to office

Many capable people do not run for office because they lack money, political connections, confidence, or the desire to pursue a public career. Elections can select for people who are unusually ambitious, highly partisan, media-skilled, or comfortable with self-promotion—not necessarily those most capable of careful public service.

A lottery would open office to citizens who would never volunteer as candidates. It could also recognize forms of knowledge that are often undervalued in politics, such as:

  • Practical workplace experience
  • Caregiving and family responsibilities
  • Local community knowledge
  • Experience with public services
  • Understanding of poverty, disability, or discrimination

7. Greater fairness in political power

Sortition embodies a strong principle of political equality: no one is presumed to have a permanent right to rule, and no citizen is permanently excluded from doing so.

Because service would be temporary and distributed across the population, political power would be less likely to become a lifelong profession or inherited social advantage. Rotation in office could limit the formation of a governing caste and reinforce the idea that public authority is a civic duty rather than a personal possession.

8. Potentially more legitimate outcomes

People may view decisions as more legitimate if they believe the decision-makers were selected fairly and reflected the population. A lottery is difficult for candidates or parties to manipulate, provided that the selection process is transparent and secure.

A representative body composed of ordinary citizens might also be more trusted on issues where the public suspects that elected politicians are serving donors, party interests, or wealthy constituencies.

Legitimacy would not come from every person voting for a specific leader, as it does in elections. It would instead come from:

  • Equal opportunity to be selected
  • Broad demographic representation
  • Transparent procedures
  • Public deliberation
  • Accountability to the wider population

9. Possible benefits for executive leadership

Sortition is most straightforward for legislatures, but advocates sometimes extend it to executive offices. Random selection could prevent executive power from being monopolized by wealthy political families, celebrities, party machines, or highly funded candidates.

A randomly selected executive council, cabinet, or citizens’ governing board might be less focused on personal political advancement and less dependent on donors. It could also provide a broader range of perspectives in executive decision-making.

However, randomly selecting a single head of government raises substantial concerns about expertise, crisis leadership, and accountability. For that reason, proposals often favor a hybrid system, such as:

  • A randomly selected legislature
  • An executive council chosen by or accountable to that legislature
  • Professional civil servants and expert advisers
  • Strict eligibility, training, and oversight rules
  • Recall, removal, or review procedures

Random selection alone would not guarantee fairness or competence. A serious nationwide system would likely need:

  • Stratified lotteries to ensure demographic and geographic representation
  • Compensation and job protection so poorer citizens can serve
  • Childcare, disability accommodations, and language access
  • Nonpartisan briefings and expert testimony
  • Transparent deliberative procedures
  • Independent ethics and anti-corruption bodies
  • Public records and media access
  • Term limits and rotation
  • Mechanisms for recall or removal for misconduct

It might make public institutions less dependent on money and parties, more socially representative, and more open to citizens who are normally excluded from political power.

The central tradeoff is that elections provide a familiar mechanism for choosing leaders and rewarding or punishing them, while sortition offers greater equality of access and potentially greater independence from elites. In Defense of Elections: Because Nothing Says “Qualified Leader” Like a Six-Month Advertising Campaign

The Wisdom of the Marketplace

Critics of sortition often explain that elections allow voters to “choose.”

This is true. Voters are offered a carefully curated menu of candidates, generally selected by political parties after an extensive process of eliminating anyone who is too strange, too honest, too independent, insufficiently photogenic, or unwilling to pretend that every issue is both incredibly urgent and completely simple.

Then citizens choose between them.

  • “The airplane pilot should be whoever raises the most money.”

Election defenders become especially alarmed at the idea of ordinary citizens serving in office.

“Random citizens might be inexperienced!” they warn.

They may not have spent twenty years learning how to avoid answering a question while appearing deeply moved by it. And a mandate is essentially a permission slip issued by millions of people who were asked which of two heavily marketed strangers they disliked less.

Some opponents of sortition argue that ordinary citizens lack the knowledge necessary to govern.

The Lottery of Liberty: Why America Must Replace Elections with Sortition

By adopting a system where leaders are chosen by chance rather than ambition, we can surgically remove political corruption, dismantle the tribal machinery of partisanship, and fundamentally empower ordinary people to reclaim the republic.

The most immediate and devastating blow of sortition would be the total eradication of political corruption and the undue influence of money. In our current electoral system, candidates must raise staggering sums of money to be viable. This creates a parasitic relationship between politicians and the wealthy donors, corporations, and lobbyists who fund their campaigns. When a representative spends 30 to 50 percent of their time dialing for dollars, they are not representing their constituents; they are servicing their donors.

Sortition destroys this dynamic instantly. Under a lottery system, there are no campaigns, no fundraising, and no reelection campaigns. A randomly selected citizen has no need for a war chest. There are no "special interests" to court because there is no next election to prepare for. Without the "pay-to-play" mechanism inherent in campaigning, the lobbyist becomes a ghost, haunting a building where no one seeks their favor. Leaders chosen by lot have no incentive to cater to the wealthy, as they cannot monetize their office for future political gain. In one swift move, we transform politics from a career of personal enrichment into a temporary civic duty, closing the revolving door between government and industry once and for all.

Furthermore, sortition is the only known cure for the venomous partisanship that threatens to tear the United States apart. Our current election system is binary and adversarial. To win an election, a candidate must distinguish themselves from their opponent, often by demonizing the "other side." This creates a zero-sum game where one party’s gain is another’s loss, fostering an environment of hatred and suspicion.

A legislature selected by lot would look like America, not like two warring tribes. Statistically, a randomly selected body naturally reflects the demographic, ideological, and socioeconomic makeup of the nation. It would include Republicans, Democrats, and Independents, but also—crucially—those who have opted out of the partisan fray. In such a body, there are no "party lines" to toe. Without the pressure of party whip or the fear of a primary challenge, randomly selected citizens are free to deliberate based on facts, conscience, and the common good. When you sit across from a neighbor selected by chance, whom you must live with in a deliberative body, the incentive shifts from "beating the opposition" to "solving the problem."

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, sortition fulfills the promise of "government by the people" in a way elections never could. Elections create a separate class of professional politicians—a political elite that often becomes detached from the realities of ordinary life. When the average age of a Senator is nearly 65 and the majority are millionaires, how can they possibly understand the struggles of a working-class single mother or a student burdened by debt?

It empowers the marginalized, ensuring that teachers, nurses, construction workers, and gig-economy drivers have a direct hand in writing the laws. This restores civic dignity. Instead of feeling like subjects watching a spectacle from the sidelines, citizens become active participants, knowing that at any moment, the civic lottery could call upon them to serve. It transforms the passive "voter" into the active "citizen-legislator."

In a modern context, we would not simply dump random people into the Capitol; we would provide them with a staff of civil servants (who remain neutral regardless of the political winds) and non-partisan briefings. Expertise is not a trait exclusive to the political class; it is a resource that can be utilized by anyone given the opportunity.

We can continue to tinker with an electoral system that grows more corrupt and polarized by the day, or we can be bold enough to return to a purer form of democracy. By replacing elections with sortition, we strip the power from the donor class, silence the echo chambers of partisan media, and hand the gavel of power to the people themselves. The concept of sortition (also known as allotment or demarchy) proposes selecting political officials through random lottery, similar to how juries are selected in many legal systems, rather than through competitive elections.

Proponents of a nationwide system of sortition argue that modern electoral systems have been corrupted by money, polarization, and professional political class interests. They suggest that sortition is a return to the original democratic ideals of ancient Athens, where it was considered more democratic than elections.

Here is an explanation of the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting sortition, specifically regarding government fairness, elite influence, and democratic representation.

1. Enhancing Democratic Representation (Statistical Accuracy)

The primary theoretical argument for sortition is that a randomly selected body will statistically resemble the population it governs. This is often referred to as descriptive representation.

  • Microcosm Theory: In an election, the winner is usually a specific demographic profile (often a wealthy, older, lawyer-politician). In a lottery, if you select 300 citizens from the general registry, the group will naturally mirror the nation's diversity. It will include roughly the same percentage of young people, retirees, factory workers, teachers, minorities, and varying political ideologies as the general public.
  • No More "Professional Politicians": Elections inherently favor those who enjoy campaigning, fundraising, and the limelight. Sortition ensures that "ordinary" citizens—who may lack charisma but possess common sense and lived experience—have a seat at the table.
  • Inclusion of the Reluctant: Elections require ambition; sortition requires only civic duty. This allows the system to capture the wisdom of those who would never run for office but have valuable perspectives to offer.

2. Reducing Elite Influence and Money in Politics

Critics of elections argue that they are effectively auctions where policy is sold to the highest bidder. Sortition is touted as a way to sever the link between wealth and power.

  • Elimination of Campaign Finance: If leaders are chosen by lottery, there are no campaigns to fund. This theoretically destroys the lobbying industry’s ability to buy influence through campaign donations, as there are no "candidates" to back.
  • Breaking the "Revolving Door": In electoral systems, politicians often legislate favorably for industries (like banking or defense) with the knowledge that they will be offered high-paying jobs in those industries after leaving office. A random citizen legislator, who returns to their normal job after a term (e.g., a plumber or nurse), has no career incentive to cater to elites.
  • Immunity to Media Manipulation: Elections rely heavily on media narratives, advertising, and spin. A lottery-selected leader does not need to appease media barons or social media algorithms to keep their job, allowing them to focus purely on policy.

3. Improving Government Fairness and Deliberation

Proponents argue that sortition changes the behavior of the government from adversarial combat to collaborative problem-solving.

  • End of Partisan Gridlock: Elections are zero-sum games (I win, you lose). This creates polarization and tribalism. Sortition creates a body that is not organized by parties. Without a "re-election" incentive, randomly selected leaders have no reason to obstruct the opposition for political gain; their only goal is to solve the problem and return home with a clean conscience.
  • True Deliberation: Electoral politics is often about "soundbites" and 30-second ads. Sortition bodies (like Citizens' Assemblies) are designed for long-form deliberation. Members are typically given time to hear expert testimony from all sides, ask questions, and debate the merits of policy without the pressure of a looming election cycle.
  • Legitimacy through Impartiality: Because the selectors have no vested interest in the outcome (unlike a politician who might gain power from a specific policy), decisions made by a sortition body are perceived as more neutral and fair by the public.

4. Restoring Public Trust

Many argue that the public is disillusioned with politics because they feel the system is "rigged."

  • Radical Transparency: Since the "politicians" are just regular people, the process of governance becomes less opaque. The mechanisms of backroom dealing become harder to maintain when the participants are random citizens who cannot be easily co-opted into a corrupt culture.
  • The "Odds" Argument: In an election, a citizen has virtually no chance of becoming a leader. In a sortition system, the possibility is real. This gives citizens a tangible stake in the system, potentially increasing civic engagement and respect for the law.

How it Would Work in Practice (The Hybrid Model)

Advocates rarely suggest firing the entire bureaucracy or abolishing the executive branch overnight. A common proposal is a Hybrid Model:

  1. The Executive/Bureaucracy: Retained as permanent, professional civil servants (experts).
  2. The Legislature: Replaced or supplemented by a sortition body.
  3. The Veto/Referendum: The public retains the right to veto laws via traditional referendums.

Criticisms and Caveats

While the benefits above are compelling in theory, it is important to note the common counter-arguments:

  • Competence: Critics argue that random people lack the expertise to handle complex issues like monetary policy, geopolitics, or constitutional law. (Proponents counter that they would rely on expert briefings, just as juries rely on legal instructions).
  • Accountability: If a lottery-selected leader acts corruptly or foolishly, they cannot be "voted out" at the next election; they simply leave when their term ends.
  • Speed: Deliberative bodies take time to reach consensus, which may be too slow during a crisis (though advocates suggest a small, elected emergency council for such scenarios).

Summary

The argument for sortition is that elections sort for the privileged and charismatic, while sortition sorts for the typical and the representative. By adopting a lottery system, a nation would theoretically replace a competitive, elite-driven hierarchy with a collaborative, statistically accurate mirror of the people themselves.

Moreover, elections create a zero-sum game in which candidates must appeal to the most ardent supporters of their party, rather than the broad center. This dynamic fosters polarization, as politicians craft messages designed to energize their base rather than build consensus. The electoral process also disproportionately advantages those with pre-existing political experience, personal wealth, or access to elite networks. Sortition—the selection of public officials by random lot—was used in ancient Athens as a primary method for choosing members of key institutions such as the Boule (council of 500), the nomothetes (lawmakers), and many other administrative bodies. The current electoral system in the United States is failing the American people. It is corrupt, polarizing, and disconnected from the needs of ordinary citizens. Model Response:

A House of the Drawn, Not the Bought: Sortition as America’s Only Remedy Against Rotten Elections

Introduction
Every four years Americans spend five-billion dollars, half a billion television ads, and countless anxious hours proving the same dreary point: the candidate who raises the most money usually wins. After two hundred and fifty years we still translate dollars into votes, then votes into power, and power into still more dollars. The circle is closed; the people are shut out. The founders gave us a republic—if we could keep it. We have not. The time has come to replace elections altogether with sortition: the random selection of lawmakers and even chief executives from the adult citizenry, exactly the way we choose juries. Only sortition breaks the iron dependency between cash and candidacy, severs the head of the permanent political class, and returns the country to government by those who must live under the laws they write. It is not utopia; it is jury duty on the scale of the nation—messy, mortal, and magnificently fair.

I. Elections Manufacture Corruption; Sortition Removes the Price Tag
Corruption is not an unfortunate side-effect of elections; corruption is the product. When candidacy itself is a scarce commodity, money naturally becomes the bidding currency. House races that cost three million dollars, Senate seats that cost twenty, presidential contests sprinting past six billion—all of it is the market-clearing price for a commodity whose supply is artificially restricted to one winner.
Sortition eliminates that commodity entirely. No one can purchase, bribe, or blackmail a person into “getting on the ballot” when there is no ballot. The pool is every adult citizen; the selector is the same blind lottery that already trusts ordinary Americans to sentence fellow citizens to life in prison. Once chosen, a legislator has neither raised a dime nor promised a favor. She arrives owing nothing to Exxon, nothing to the teachers-union Super-PAC, nothing to the consulting class that normally writes the ads, the bills, even the post-office names. Bribery cannot target the next election when there is no next election; influence peddlers cannot groom a career that ends at the close of a single fixed term.

II. Partisanship as a Cartel: Elections Sustain It, Sortition Dissolves It
Political parties are not civic charities; they are cartels that rig the labor market for power. By controlling ballot access, debate rules, gerrymandered maps, and rivers of donor cash, Republicans and Democrats operate exactly like OPEC fixing oil prices—only the commodity here is legislation. Partisan identity is then sold back to voters as a poisonous social identity: “I am Red, you are Blue; therefore you are my enemy.”
Sortition breaks the cartel’s toolkit overnight. Random selection produces a body whose partisan distribution mirrors the country—about a third Democrats, a quarter Republicans, two-fifths independents, plus Libertarians, Greens, the apolitical and the alienated. With no party gatekeepers, the assembly begins where the electorate already is: ideologically diverse and sick of the show. Deliberation is no longer a staged wrestling match for cable news but a search for common policy ground among citizens who must fly home to the same grocery shortages and ER wait times as the rest of us. Ireland’s 2012–14 Citizens’ Assembly (randomly selected but purely advisory) delivered near-unanimous recommendations on marriage equality and abortion that the elected parliament feared to touch for decades. Imagine that power made binding, expanded to every law.

III. The Common-Sense Competence of Ordinary Americans
Skeptics sneer that random selection will seat “incompetents.” The condescension is revealing: we already trust twelve random jurors to/confiscate property, split families, or sentence to death; we trust randomly selected parents to run a $100-million school board; we trust random privates to launch nuclear missiles. Yet we cannot trust a statistically representative sample to decide the federal gas tax?
Modern social science says we can. In deliberative mini-publics from Australia to Mongolia, ordinary citizens—given balanced briefing materials, expert Q&A, and time—outperform elected chambers in factual knowledge, policy consistency, and post-deliberation consensus. Cognitive diversity beats elite homogeneity: a plumbers-and-teachers legislature will contain more electricians than Harvard graduates, more Medicaid recipients than Goldman partners. The former know what a 40-cent copper fitting costs, how an EPA permit can kill a small-contract deadline, what it feels like when the pharmacy is out of insulin. The country’s real competence lies in that distributed intelligence, not in the debating-club narcissists who currently self-select for office.

IV. Sortition for the Executive: A Stabilizing Rotation
Critics gasp, “Sure, legislatures by lottery—but the President?” Yes, even the President. Ancient Athens rotated entire executive committees (the “archons”) by lot; Renaissance Venice chose its head of state—the Doge—through a deliberately complex quasi-randomizing procedure that kept the city stable for a thousand years while the crowned heads of Europe toppled around it.
Design options abound. One model: after an initial medical, security-clearance, and conflict-of-interest screening (identical to the filters already applied to jurors or draftees), a short random list of, say, fifty citizens is drawn. Those fifty participate in a three-month, televised civic-academy: constitutional law, macro-economics, foreign policy. They may withdraw without stigma. From the remaining pool a final single name is drawn to serve one non-renewable six-year term. A dovetail Vice-President could be simultaneously drawn to guard against mortality. Crucially, the new chief executive lands indebted to no donor, no early-state primary king-maker, no media conglomerate that sold ad time at 3 a.m. in Des Moines. She governs beside a Cabinet half composed of technocratic professionals (also randomly selected from pre-vetted lists) and half of ordinary citizens—ensuring that OSHA regulations are written by people who once worked in an actual warehouse.

V. Safeguards and Checks: Learning from Athens Without Repeating Its Faults
Sortition is not the abolition of checks and balances; it is their democratization. A few key guardrails:

  1. Fixed Single Terms: No re-selection, hence no incentive to campaign while governing.
  2. Mandatory Rotation: One-quarter of both legislative chambers turns over every year, preserving institutional memory while preventing entrenchment.
  3. Veto by Supreme Court and Referendum: Courts retain judicial review; citizens may nullify any statute via a 1-percent-triggered referendum within 90 days.
  4. Post-Service Audit: Every ex-official undergoes the same financial-disclosure and conflict audit applied to military officers. Hidden bribes discovered later trigger confiscation plus treble damages—paid personally, not by taxpayers.
  5. Professional Staff Permanence: Committees maintain non-partisan civil-service staff to ensure continuity and technical expertise. The elected may write the laws; unelected technocrats merely explain their consequences.

VI. Answering the “Cuckoo” Counter-Arguments

  1. “We’ll get the village idiot.” Statistically impossible. A 500-person House drawn from 250 million adults has a one-in-a-trillion chance of seating a majority with IQs below 90. Even if one arrives, current Congress already contains dunderheads who win with 96% incumbency rates. The difference under sortition is that the dunderhead cannot trade her vote for a beach-house.
  2. “No accountability.” False. Elections feel good but produce almost zero ex-post accountability: ninety-five percent of incumbents win, and once retired they cash in. Under sortition, every official knows that the law they pass will apply to them personally in ten months when they rejoin civilian life. That is a tighter feedback loop than any ballot box.
  3. “Special interests will just lobby the randoms.” Lobbying survives, but its ROI collapses. Instead of bribing a career committee chair whose son interned at your PAC, you now must wine-and-dine 200 rotating, anonymous citizens who legally must disclose every free sandwich and who leave office in twelve months. The lobbying industry would wither like Christmas tinsel.
  4. “Minorities will be underrepresented.” Mathematics says otherwise. A random sample of 500 citizens includes, on average, sixty Black, eighty Latino, twenty-five Asian-American members—proportional mirrors of the nation. Compare today’s Senate: 3% Black in a 13% Black country. Sortition outperforms elections on minority inclusion without any quota.
  5. “Americans won’t serve.” Ninety-five percent already show up for jury duty when summoned. For those who refuse, we apply the same small fines levied today. In any event, a modest stipend keyed to median household income (say, $120,000/year plus housing) would make civic duty attractive, not punitive.

VII. Steps to Transition: From Here to the Draw without Bloodshed

  1. Constitutional Amendment: Start small—one hundred randomly chosen “People’s Senators” added to the existing Senate, serving three-year terms. Require both chambers to adopt any tax increase or declaration of war only after the People’s Senate concurs. Let the country watch the sky fail to fall.
  2. Parallel People’s Assemblies in Ten States: Use the same lottery to craft redistricting maps, budgets, and climate plans. Citizens will quickly prefer the wisdom of the chamber that includes their barber and their kid’s science teacher over the chamber of millionaires.
  3. National Convention Phase: After two electoral cycles, convene a new Constitutional Convention whose delegates are themselves randomly selected. Task them with drafting the full replacement charter for sortitive Congress and Presidency. Because the delegates are statistically us, popular ratification follows.
  4. Sunset Elections: The amendment specifies that after, say, twelve years every elected office converts to sortition, giving current politicians a dignified off-ramp while reassuring the public of an orderly wind-down.

VIII. The Moral Stakes: Recovering Citizen Equality
The Declaration of Independence grounds legitimacy on the “consent of the governed.” Yet elections today secure no such consent; at best they secure 51% of 55% of the electorate—barely a quarter of adults. Sortition restores literal political equality: every citizen’s name sits in the same drum. The teenager serving fries, the octogenarian on dialysis, the Afghan-war vet, the Dreamer-turned-citizen—all have an identical probability of shaping the next farm bill. That mathematical equality is the only condition under which obedience to law is morally obligatory, for then the law is literally self-imposed. Anything less is oligarchy dressed in red-white-and-blue bunting.

Conclusion
We stand at the exhausted end of an experiment that began in 1789: the belief that competitive elections would filter ambition and produce wisdom. The evidence is in. Elections have degenerated into auctions, the citizen into a target demographic, the republic into a family business whose heirs are named Clinton, Bush, Kennedy, McConnell, Pelosi. A technology two thousand years old—selection by lot—now offers the sole reliable algorithm to bleach corruption, drain partisan poison, and seat a Congress that looks like America instead of like a reunion at Phillips Exeter. Sortition is not a leap into the dark; it is a step back onto the firm ground of citizen equality, the ground on which the republic was first imagined. Let us finally walk that ground again. Draw the lots, open the assembly, and rediscover government of ourselves, by ourselves, for ourselves—before the last dollar drowns the last vote.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt a nationwide system of sortition—random lottery selection of legislative and executive leaders—instead of using traditional elections, focusing on how it might improve government fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation.
Model Response:

Why have a national lottery for Congress and even the White House?
Because the core disease of electoral democracy is not the voters – it is the campaign. Elections force every would-be representative to become a full-time fund-raiser, brand-builder and spin-master. The skills that win races are not the skills that solve problems, and the money, media attention and organizational muscle required to win races are supplied by a tiny, highly organized stratum of society. Sortition removes the campaign. By installing a statistically random slice of the population you simultaneously (1) make the legislature a mirror instead of a filter, (2) unplug the channels through which elites convert economic power into political power, and (3) create a deliberative body whose legitimacy rests on the fact that any citizen could have been chosen, not on the fact that they defeated someone else.

Below are the main benefits that advocates claim would follow from replacing elections with sortition for one or both chambers of the federal legislature, and – in the most radical proposals – for a collegial executive drawn by lot as well.

  1. Descriptive fairness: the Assembly finally looks like the country

A random sample of 500 Americans will, with 99 % certainty, contain:

  • 250 women
  • 60–70 Black, 60–70 Latinx, 15–20 Asian-American members
  • 60–80 people without a four-year degree
  • 60 people who today make under $30 k
  • 15–20 veterans, 30–40 small-business owners, 15–20 farmers, 15–20 disabled people, etc.

No gerrymander, quota rule or campaign-finance law can guarantee that level of descriptive accuracy; probability theory does it automatically. Descriptive presence matters because empirical studies of deliberative mini-publics show that when a group “looks like us” participants trust the outcome even when they personally lost the vote; losers consent.

  1. Elimination of the campaign-money bottleneck

Under sortition no one can buy television time, hire consultants or build name recognition in advance, because there is no campaign. The price of entering politics therefore falls from the current $1.5 million (average cost of a winning House race) to the opportunity cost of serving for a fixed term. The transfer of billions of dollars from donors, lobbyists and parties to candidates simply disappears, which collapses the main present-day pipeline that converts economic inequality into political inequality. Incumbent wealth is still allowed – the lottery can pick a billionaire – but it cannot be deployed strategically because ex-ante spending is irrelevant.

  1. Term limits and rotation that cannot be gamed

Electoral term limits always leave open the possibility that the same elite migrates from one office to another (the “Musical Chairs” problem). Sortition enforces rotation: once you have served you go back into the pool with the same probability as everyone else. The expected number of life-time legislators in a 500-seat chamber sampled from 250 million adults is … 0.0002. Political careers become an accident, not a profession, and the ecosystem of aides, consultants and party bureaucrats whose livelihood depends on permanent re-election campaigns shrinks accordingly.

  1. Cognitive and epistemic diversity

Random selection maximizes group diversity on every attribute that is uncorrelated with the sampling process. In practice that means more electricians, nurses, truck-drivers, social workers and wait-staff – people whose lived experience gives them tacit knowledge about how regulation feels on the ground. Political scientists who have run “citizens’ juries” document a measurable shift in agenda topics once the share of non-professionals exceeds roughly one third: transportation, housing, energy and care-work move up; abstract ideological grand-standing moves down.

  1. Incentives aligned with the public good

An elected representative must worry about the next election; a randomly selected citizen-legislator cannot stand again and therefore internalizes the long-term consequences of policy. The single-term incentive is analogous to the difference between a tenure decision and a quarterly-earnings call. Empirical evidence from randomly selected local school-board members in Swiss cantons shows that they vote for higher investment financed by debt that matures well beyond their term – exactly the inter-generational behavior standard theory says democracies fail to deliver.

  1. Civilizing effect on public deliberation

Because the chamber is a random sample, the probability that your own child, sibling or neighbor will sit in it next year is non-trivial. That thought experiment disciplines the kind of rhetoric citizens are willing to endorse. When Ireland used a randomly selected “Citizens’ Assembly” to break a 35-year deadlock on abortion, post-deliberation polls showed that 37 % of voters changed their minds, but only 2 % felt “angry” about the outcome – an unheard-of ratio for a moral wedge issue.

  1. Reduction of zero-sum partisan identity

Elections create a permanent class of strategic elites who profit from polarization. Sortition replaces conflict over WHO rules with deliberation over WHAT rules, because the personnel is exogenously given. Without the need to “win tomorrow,” the payoff to demonization falls and cross-group coalitions become the only way to assemble a majority inside the chamber.

  1. Built-in protection against authoritarian populism

Populists succeed by convincing a plurality that “the elite” has stolen democracy. A legislature sitting by lot is the physical refutation of that claim: you can literally see that the farmer from Kansas, the Uber driver from Atlanta and the teacher from Maine are writing the laws. Historical evidence from Athens and from modern Italian city-states that used sortition shows that coups become harder when the public believes the incumbent body is “us,” not “them.”

  1. Cheaper, faster and simpler logistics

Running a national lottery every two years costs the same as running the Powerball (≈ $80 m) – four orders of magnitude less than the $14 bn Americans now spend on federal elections every cycle. The administrative apparatus is already in place in every state: motor-voter files, social-security numbers, the selective-service database. Compliance is automatic: if your number comes up you serve unless you claim an exemption (care-giver, military deployment, criminal conviction). No registration drives, no get-out-the-vote logistics, no recounts, no hanging chads.

  1. Psychological reclaiming of citizenship

Elections turn most citizens into spectators whose main political act is choosing among options pre-packaged by professionals. Sortition turns every citizen into a potential legislator. Survey experiments in which respondents are told “Next year 300 Americans will be chosen by lot to rewrite the farm bill; your chance of being picked is 1 in 600 000” produce a statistically significant jump in factual political knowledge and internal efficacy the next day. The mere possibility of service educates.

Addressing the obvious objections

Competence – Modern proposals never drop untrained citizens straight into the Capitol. A typical blueprint is:

  1. Randomly draw a pool 5–10× larger than the chamber.
  2. Pay each draftee a modest stipend to attend two weekends of orientation where they meet legislative staff, budget analysts, constitutional scholars.
  3. Allow self-exclusion or medical excuse, then re-randomize down to the final assembly.
  4. Give the assembly the same committee staff, CRS, GAO and Congressional Budget Office resources elected members have today.
  5. Make votes secret until the term ends if you want to insulate members from lobbyists.

The result is a body whose average member knows no less about public policy after six months than the average freshman representative who arrived via election.

Representation of minorities – If you want to be absolutely certain that Blacks, Latinos, veterans or the disabled cross some threshold, stratify the lottery instead of using simple random sampling. Statisticians do this every night for the Nielsen TV sample; the mathematics is trivial and the Supreme Court has already approved stratified juries.

Executive function – For the presidency, multi-member sortition is the safest approach: a seven-person “executive council” drawn by lot, serving single seven-year staggered terms, with one member rotating in as nominal chair each year. This keeps the decisive body small enough to act but large enough that a single unqualified person cannot crash the system. All adoptive democracies that switched from elected to collegial presidencies (Switzerland, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the European Commission) saw a decline in personalized populism.

Accountability – Accountability is ex-post rather than ex-ante. Randomly selected legislators know they will return to live under the laws they passed; their post-service earnings prospects are identical to those of any other citizen. That is a material incentive not to ruin the country. Empirically, financial conflict-of-interest violations among randomly selected local officials in Swiss and German councils are 40–70 % lower than among their elected colleagues.

Bottom line

Sortition is not a utopian guess; it is a technology already nested inside the most trusted institution Americans have – the jury – and it is the only institutional reform that attacks the supply side of political inequality without curtailing speech or spending. By removing the campaign, it removes the primary mechanism whereby economic elites, media conglomerates and ideological factions convert their advantages into law. What is left is a legislature that is poorer, shorter, more ordinary and – paradoxically – more legitimate precisely because no one hustled for the job.

Title: A Nation by Chance: Why Sortition Could Save American Democracy

Introduction

The United States has long prided itself on a democratic system built around regular elections. Yet the very mechanisms that were meant to guarantee representation have, over time, become conduits for corruption, partisan gridlock, and elite domination. Imagine a political landscape where the ordinary citizen—not a career politician or a well‑funded campaign—holds the reins of power. Sortition, the random selection of citizens to serve in legislative and executive roles, offers precisely that vision. By replacing elections with a carefully designed sortition system, the United States could dramatically diminish corruption, dissolve entrenched partisanship, and restore genuine political agency to its people.

1. Sortition Eliminates the Primary Engine of Corruption

a. Money No Longer Determines Access
Elections are fundamentally contests of resources. Campaign finance laws have failed to curb the influence of wealthy donors, super‑PACs, and corporate lobbyists. Candidates spend billions courting donors, and elected officials feel indebted to those who financed their victories. In a sortition system, there is no campaign, no fundraising, and no donor‑politician relationship to exploit. Citizens are chosen at random, receive a modest stipend, and are insulated from the financial pressures that currently shape policy decisions.

b. Transparency and Accountability Through Randomness
When a public office is filled by lottery, the selection process itself is transparent and auditable. Citizens can witness the draw, verify that it is truly random, and trust that no hidden back‑room deals have taken place. Moreover, because the tenure is short and the pool of office‑holders constantly rotates, opportunities for long‑term entrenchment and corrupt networks are dramatically reduced. A corrupt official can only wield influence for a limited period before being replaced by a fresh citizen.

c. Reduced Lobbying Power
Lobbyists thrive on the predictability of elected officials who must constantly seek re‑election. With sortition, legislators are not beholden to any voting base, and they have no incentive to cultivate relationships with lobbyists for future campaign support. While lobbying will not disappear entirely, its leverage will be curtailed because decision‑makers no longer need to protect a political career.

2. Sortition Dismantles Partisan Polarization

a. No Party Labels, No Party Loyalty
Elections are organized around parties, which package complex policy debates into simplified, often polarizing, slogans. Parties incentivize legislators to toe the party line, even when it conflicts with the public interest. In a sortition system, officials are not members of a party; they are independent citizens. Without party whips, committee chairs, or primary battles, the pressure to conform to a partisan agenda evaporates.

b. Cross‑Cutting Social Representation
Random selection ensures that the body of decision‑makers mirrors the demographic, geographic, and socioeconomic diversity of the nation. When a legislature includes farmers, teachers, engineers, retirees, and people from every region, the natural outcome is a richer, more nuanced discussion of policy. This diversity breaks the echo chambers that fuel partisan echoing and forces legislators to consider viewpoints they would otherwise ignore.

c. Collaborative Governance Over Competition
Elected bodies are structured around competition for votes and the next election cycle. Sortition replaces competition with collaboration: each cohort of citizens works together for a fixed term, knowing that they will be succeeded by a new, equally random group. The incentive shifts from winning the next campaign to solving problems efficiently for the public good.

3. Sortition Empowers Ordinary People

a. Direct Participation and Civic Education
When any eligible citizen can be called to serve, the prospect of public office becomes a shared civic responsibility rather than a career path reserved for the politically ambitious. Citizens will be more motivated to stay informed about public affairs, knowing that they could be summoned to serve at any time. This fosters a culture of lifelong learning and engagement that elections, which often leave the majority disengaged, cannot match.

b. Breaking the Professional Politician Class
In the current system, politics has become a profession: a small class of career politicians dominates the halls of power, often detached from everyday experiences. Sortition dismantles this class by rotating ordinary citizens through office. The resulting “citizen‑legislators” bring real‑world perspectives to policy‑making, ensuring that laws reflect the lived realities of the populace rather than the abstract interests of a political elite.

c. Restoring Trust in Government
Public trust in political institutions has been in decline for decades, largely because citizens perceive elected officials as self‑interested and beholden to special interests. A sortition system, by its very design, signals that power is a public trust, not a private prize. When people see their neighbors, coworkers, or fellow community members serving in government, the sense that “government is for us” is revived.

4. Practical Safeguards for a Sortition‑Based Republic

  1. Eligibility and Randomization – All citizens over the age of 18, without criminal convictions, would be entered into a national database. A transparent, computer‑generated lottery would draw a statistically representative sample for each office.
  2. Term Limits and Rotation – Legislative terms could be set at two years, with staggered cohorts to ensure continuity while preventing long‑term entrenchment. Executive roles (e.g., President, Governor) could be filled by a short‑term “citizen‑cabinet” that rotates annually.
  3. Support Structures – Selected citizens would receive professional briefings, staff assistance, and modest remuneration to enable them to perform effectively without financial hardship.
  4. Oversight Mechanisms – An independent, non‑partisan audit board would monitor the lottery process, enforce eligibility rules, and investigate any attempts at manipulation.
  5. Hybrid Transition – To preserve stability, the United States could adopt a phased approach: beginning with sortition panels for advisory commissions, then for certain legislative chambers (e.g., a “citizen senate”), and finally extending the model to executive offices.

These safeguards preserve the core democratic principle that power lies with the people, while ensuring competence, accountability, and continuity.

5. Counterarguments Addressed

  • “Random citizens lack expertise.”
    Expertise is not a prerequisite for sound judgment; it can be supplied through briefings, expert testimonies, and collaborative deliberation. Moreover, the diversity of backgrounds among randomly selected citizens often yields creative solutions that specialists may overlook.

  • “Sortition undermines legitimacy.”
    Legitimacy stems from public consent. A transparent lottery, openly observed by the nation, provides a clear and indisputable source of legitimacy—far more than the opaque influence of money in elections.

  • “It would be chaotic.”
    Existing democratic institutions already manage complexity; adding a structured, well‑designed sortition process would not increase chaos but would replace the chaotic influence of money and partisan maneuvering with predictable, rule‑based selection.

  • “Constitutional constraints.”
    The Constitution can be amended through the established process, just as it has been amended to expand suffrage, abolish slavery, and grant voting rights to women. The same democratic mechanisms can be employed to adopt sortition.

Conclusion

The United States stands at a crossroads. Its electoral system, once a beacon of democratic innovation, now fuels corruption, entrenches partisanship, and distances ordinary citizens from the levers of power. Sortition offers a bold, evidence‑based alternative that directly confronts these maladies. By randomizing the selection of legislators and executives, we eliminate the money‑driven incentives that corrupt politics, dissolve the party structures that polarize debate, and return political agency to the people themselves.

A nation that chooses its leaders by chance, not by campaign, would embody the original spirit of a republic “of the people, by the people, for the people.” It would be a living experiment in true democratic equality—one that could finally deliver on the promise that every citizen, not just the well‑connected, has an equal stake in shaping the future of the United States.

The time has come to let chance, not cash, decide our destiny.

Replacing Elections with Sortition: A Stronger Democracy Through Citizen Selection

The United States often describes itself as the world’s leading democracy, yet its political system has become increasingly distorted by money, permanent campaigning, partisan tribalism, and public distrust. Elections are supposed to give ordinary citizens control over government. In practice, however, they often reward those with the greatest access to wealth, media attention, party machinery, and professional political networks. The result is a system in which many Americans feel that government is not truly theirs, but rather belongs to donors, lobbyists, political consultants, and career politicians.

A bold but deeply democratic alternative exists: sortition, the selection of public officials by random lottery from the citizenry. Instead of choosing leaders through expensive, divisive elections, the United States should replace electoral politics with a carefully designed system of random citizen selection for legislative and executive offices. Under sortition, ordinary Americans would be called to serve in government much as they are called to serve on juries. With proper training, expert support, transparency, and accountability, randomly selected citizens could deliberate, govern, and make decisions in the public interest.

This would not be a retreat from democracy. It would be a restoration of democracy. Sortition would reduce political corruption, weaken destructive partisanship, and empower ordinary people far more effectively than the current electoral system.

Elections Have Become a Gateway for Corruption

The first and most urgent argument for sortition is that it would strike at the heart of political corruption. Modern American elections require enormous sums of money. Candidates for Congress, governorships, and the presidency must spend much of their time raising funds, courting donors, building alliances with interest groups, and appealing to wealthy networks capable of financing campaigns. Even when no explicit bribery occurs, the system creates a powerful dependence on money.

This dependence shapes political behavior. Candidates learn which positions attract donations and which ones provoke well-funded opposition. They understand that angering major industries, wealthy donors, or influential lobbying organizations can end a campaign. As a result, policy is often filtered through the question of what is politically and financially viable, not simply what is just, necessary, or beneficial to the public.

Sortition would radically disrupt this dynamic. A randomly selected citizen would not need to raise campaign funds. They would not owe their position to donors, party leaders, political action committees, or media strategists. They would enter office without a campaign debt to repay. There would be no need to spend years cultivating wealthy backers or making quiet promises to special interests.

Lobbying would not disappear entirely, of course. Powerful groups would still try to influence policy. But sortition would make influence harder to concentrate and easier to regulate. Instead of targeting a permanent political class whose ambitions and vulnerabilities are well known, lobbyists would face rotating bodies of ordinary citizens selected for limited terms. Those citizens would have less incentive to build long-term relationships with special interests because they would not be running for reelection. Strong conflict-of-interest rules, transparency requirements, public financing of government research, and strict anti-bribery laws could further protect the process.

In an electoral system, politicians often think about the next campaign. In a sortition system, citizen-legislators could think about the next generation.

Sortition Would Reduce Partisan Warfare

The second major advantage of sortition is that it would reduce the extreme partisanship that now dominates American politics. Elections force society into teams. Candidates must distinguish themselves from opponents, mobilize loyal supporters, and often portray the other side as dangerous or immoral. Political parties then amplify these divisions because their survival depends on winning and holding power.

The result is a permanent campaign culture. Every issue becomes a partisan symbol. Every compromise is framed as betrayal. Every legislative debate becomes an opportunity to generate outrage, raise money, and energize a political base. In this environment, politicians are punished for honest uncertainty and rewarded for ideological performance.

Sortition changes the incentives. Randomly selected citizens would not need to appeal to partisan primary voters. They would not need to produce viral sound bites or attack ads. They would not have to satisfy party donors or cable news audiences. Instead, they could be organized into deliberative bodies where the goal is not victory over an opposing party, but collective judgment.

Ordinary citizens, when placed in structured deliberative settings, are often more practical and less ideologically rigid than professional politicians. Most Americans are not full-time partisans. They hold mixed views, care about local realities, and are capable of listening when given time, information, and responsibility. A citizen selected by lot from Ohio, Arizona, Georgia, or Maine may have political leanings, but they are unlikely to have built an entire career around partisan warfare.

A sortition-based Congress could be designed to reflect the actual diversity of the country: urban and rural, rich and poor, young and old, religious and secular, conservative and progressive, immigrant and native-born. Rather than reducing Americans to two hostile camps, sortition would bring them together as citizens with shared responsibility.

This does not mean disagreement would vanish. Democracy requires disagreement. But sortition would make disagreement less performative and more constructive. It would move politics from campaign combat to civic deliberation.

Sortition Empowers Ordinary People

The deepest democratic argument for sortition is that it gives ordinary people real power. Elections promise popular sovereignty, but most citizens participate only by voting every few years for candidates they did not choose, funded by donors they do not know, operating within parties they may not trust. The average voter has a tiny influence over outcomes, while professional politicians and organized interests dominate the agenda.

Sortition would transform citizenship from passive observation into active responsibility. Any eligible citizen could be selected to serve. Government would no longer be the preserve of lawyers, wealthy candidates, political insiders, and media-trained personalities. Teachers, nurses, mechanics, farmers, engineers, small-business owners, warehouse workers, parents, retirees, and students could all become lawmakers or public executives.

This would make government more representative in a genuine social sense. Elected bodies often fail to resemble the people they govern. They are usually wealthier, more credentialed, more politically connected, and more professionally ambitious than the general population. Sortition, by contrast, can produce a governing body that mirrors the country. If selection is properly stratified to ensure demographic balance, it can reflect America’s real composition far better than elections do.

Critics may say ordinary people are not qualified to govern. But this objection misunderstands both democracy and expertise. Ordinary citizens already make serious decisions on juries, in local institutions, in workplaces, in families, in military service, and in community organizations. They are capable of learning, deliberating, and judging evidence. They do not need to be experts in every policy area; they need access to experts, staff, data, and time for thoughtful decision-making.

Indeed, elected politicians are often not experts either. They rely on staff, agencies, consultants, lobbyists, and think tanks. The difference is that elected politicians must constantly balance public duty against political survival. Randomly selected citizens, freed from reelection pressures, could focus more directly on the merits of policy.

A government of ordinary citizens would also restore public trust. People are more likely to believe in a system when they see people like themselves making decisions. Sortition communicates a powerful democratic message: the nation belongs to all of us, not merely to those who can win campaigns.

Executive Leadership Could Also Be Chosen by Sortition

Some may accept sortition for legislatures but hesitate when it comes to executive leadership. The presidency, governorships, and mayoralties involve administration, crisis response, and coordination. But elections do not guarantee competence in executive office. They often select for charisma, ambition, fundraising skill, ideological branding, and media performance—not administrative wisdom.

A sortition-based executive system could be designed responsibly. Instead of selecting a single unprepared citizen and handing them unchecked power, the country could create citizen executive councils. These councils would be randomly selected from eligible citizens, screened for basic capacity and conflicts of interest, trained extensively, and supported by professional civil servants. They could appoint qualified administrators, oversee agencies, and make high-level decisions collectively.

Emergency powers could require supermajority approval or temporary delegation to trained officials under strict oversight. The military, intelligence agencies, and federal bureaucracy would remain professionalized but accountable to the citizen executive body.

Such a system would avoid the dangerous concentration of power in one personality. It would also reduce the cult of celebrity that has overtaken executive elections. Presidents govern with constant attention to approval ratings, media cycles, partisan narratives, and the next election. Policy decisions become campaign tools.

Sortition would end this permanent campaign. There would be no campaign advertisements, no primary battles, no gerrymandering, no voter suppression, no partisan redistricting wars, no billionaire-funded election machines, and no endless speculation about electability. The strongest objection to sortition is accountability. If citizens do not elect leaders, how can they remove bad ones? This is a serious concern, but elections are not the only form of accountability—and often not the best one.

A sortition system could include multiple safeguards:

  1. Short, fixed terms so no citizen-official remains in power too long.
  2. Recall by independent review panels in cases of corruption, abuse, or incapacity.
  3. Strict transparency rules requiring public records, open deliberations where appropriate, and published explanations of major decisions.
  4. Ethics enforcement with severe penalties for bribery or conflicts of interest.
  5. Rotation of service to prevent the formation of a new political class.
  6. Independent courts to protect constitutional rights.
  7. Citizen oversight bodies selected by lot to monitor government performance.
  8. Referendums for major constitutional changes or extraordinary national decisions.

By contrast, sortition can rely on immediate legal, ethical, and institutional accountability.

The purpose of democracy is not merely to allow voters to punish leaders after damage has been done. It is to design institutions that make corruption, domination, and irresponsibility less likely in the first place.

Elections naturally favor inequality. People with money, fame, elite education, party connections, and polished communication skills have enormous advantages. It recognizes that political wisdom is not confined to those who seek power. In fact, those who do not seek power may be more trustworthy precisely because they are not driven by ambition.

This is one of sortition’s greatest virtues: it separates public office from the hunger for public office. Elections reward those who want power badly enough to campaign for it. Sortition asks citizens to serve because their community needs them. That difference is profound.

The United States does not need more expensive campaigns, sharper partisan warfare, or deeper dependence on political donors. It needs a democratic system that trusts ordinary people, reduces corruption, and encourages public reason. Sortition offers that possibility.

By replacing elections with random citizen selection, America could free government from the grip of campaign finance, weaken the power of political parties, and bring ordinary citizens directly into the work of governing. It would create institutions that look more like the country itself and less like a permanent ruling class. It would make public office a civic duty rather than a career prize.

Elections once seemed like the highest expression of democracy. But in the modern United States, they too often produce manipulation, corruption, and division. Sortition would revive an older and more radical democratic principle: government by the people, not merely government chosen from among professional politicians.

A nation that truly believes in the wisdom and dignity of its citizens should be willing to let them govern. Sortition is not anti-democratic. It is democracy taken seriously.

The Case for Sortition: Reclaiming Democracy Through Random Selection

Introduction

American democracy stands at a crossroads. Trust in government has plummeted to historic lows. Congress operates with approval ratings that would embarrass a used car salesman. Money floods our political system like water through a broken dam, and partisan gridlock has transformed governance into perpetual warfare rather than problem-solving. It is time to consider a radical but historically grounded solution: replacing elections with sortition—the random selection of citizens to serve in legislative and executive roles. This system, used successfully in ancient Athens and increasingly piloted in modern democracies, offers a genuine path toward the government "of the people, by the people, for the people" that our founding documents promised but our electoral system has failed to deliver.

The Corruption Problem: Elections Are Bought, Not Won

Modern American elections have become auctions disguised as democratic exercises. The 2020 federal elections cost over $14 billion—money that flows overwhelmingly from wealthy donors, corporations, and special interests expecting returns on their investment. Politicians spend an estimated 30-70% of their time fundraising rather than legislating, creating permanent dependency on donor class approval.

Sortition eliminates this corruption at its root. When leadership is chosen randomly, there is no campaign to fund, no donor to please, and no reelection to secure through favorable votes. A citizen selected through sortition owes nothing to anyone—not to a party, not to a PAC, not to a billionaire donor. They arrive in office as a blank slate, accountable only to their conscience and their fellow citizens. Corruption requires leverage; sortition removes the very mechanisms that create it.

Ending the Partisan Death Spiral

American politics has become a tribal battlefield where policy takes a backseat to party loyalty. Gerrymandering has created safe districts where representatives fear primary challengers more than general election opponents, pushing politicians toward ideological extremes. The two-party duopoly has calcified into warring camps more interested in denying the other side victories than governing effectively.

Sortition shatters this dynamic entirely. A randomly selected legislature would reflect the actual demographic, ideological, and geographic diversity of the nation—not the artificial binary that our electoral system manufactures. Without parties controlling nominations, without primaries rewarding extremism, and without campaign war chests determining viability, the entire infrastructure of partisan warfare collapses. Citizens selected by lot would need to build consensus based on merit and argument rather than party discipline, because there would be no party enforcing discipline in the first place.

Empowering Ordinary People, Not Just Political Elites

Our current system all but guarantees that only a narrow slice of Americans can realistically hold office: the wealthy, the well-connected, the charismatic performers who excel at fundraising and media appearances. Working-class Americans, single parents, people without expensive educations, and those who simply hate the ugliness of modern campaigning are systematically excluded from governance—not by law, but by the practical realities of how elections function.

Sortition is radically democratic in the truest sense. It says that a warehouse worker in Ohio, a nurse in Arizona, a farmer in Iowa, and a teacher in Georgia are all equally capable of contributing to self-governance as any career politician or wealthy lawyer. This isn't merely idealistic—it reflects genuine trust in citizens' collective wisdom, an idea our founders themselves championed even as they built an imperfect electoral system. James Madison and Alexis de Tocqueville both recognized that a broad citizenry, when given proper information and deliberation, could reason toward sound judgment. Sortition operationalizes this faith by ensuring government truly resembles the governed.

Historical Precedent and Modern Success

Skeptics might dismiss sortition as untested fantasy, but history and contemporary practice suggest otherwise. Athenian democracy, often cited as history's foundational democratic model, relied heavily on sortition for selecting officials, jurors, and council members precisely because Athenians distrusted the corrupting potential of elections, which they associated with oligarchy and demagoguery.

More recently, Ireland's Citizens' Assembly—a sortition-based body—successfully tackled contentious issues like abortion and marriage equality, producing recommendations that were then ratified through referendum. These deliberative bodies consistently demonstrate that ordinary citizens, given adequate information, expert testimony, and structured deliberation time, produce thoughtful, balanced policy recommendations that often exceed the quality of legislation produced by professional politicians beholden to donors and party lines.

Addressing the Objections

Critics will raise legitimate concerns, but each has workable solutions. Will randomly selected citizens have adequate expertise? Modern sortition proposals include mandatory training periods, access to expert testimony, and professional staff support—similar to how jurors receive guidance from judges without being legal experts themselves. Will accountability suffer without reelection incentives? Sortition can incorporate performance reviews, term limits, and even random citizen oversight panels to ensure officials serve responsibly, freed from reelection pressure but not from accountability altogether.

Will chosen citizens simply defer to unelected bureaucrats or lobbyists? This risk exists in our current system regardless, and arguably sortition reduces it—professional bureaucrats currently exploit politicians' need for expertise and their fundraising distractions. Ordinary citizens with fresh eyes and no career stakes in pleasing permanent Washington power structures may prove more resistant to institutional capture, not less.

Conclusion

The Case for Sortition: Why Random Citizen Selection Must Replace All Elections in the United States

The American political system is not broken by accident—it is broken by design. Elections, once envisioned as the noble mechanism of self-government, have devolved into an expensive, corrupting, and deeply unrepresentative spectacle that rewards the most ambitious, most connected, and most extreme candidates while sidelining the vast majority of ordinary citizens. It is time to admit a difficult truth: elections are incompatible with genuine democracy in a modern mass society. The solution is not campaign finance reform, term limits, or yet another round of hopeful tinkering. The solution is to replace all elections—at the federal, state, and local levels—with sortition: the random selection of legislative and executive leaders from the citizen body itself.

Sortition, sometimes called “citizens’ assemblies” or “allotment,” is not a radical new theory. It was the central mechanism of the world’s first democracy in ancient Athens, where most public offices were filled by lottery rather than election. Far from producing chaos, it produced one of the most dynamic and resilient societies in history. Today, modern implementations—such as citizens’ assemblies in Ireland, Canada, and elsewhere—have shown that randomly selected citizens can deliberate thoughtfully, reach cross-partisan consensus, and make better decisions than professional politicians on complex issues. It is time to scale this proven method to the entire American system of government.

Sortition eliminates the root cause of political corruption.

The most corrosive force in American politics is not incompetence or ideology—it is money. Running for Congress or the presidency requires raising millions or billions of dollars. This creates an unbreakable dependency on donors, lobbyists, special interests, and super PACs. Even well-intentioned politicians must spend hours every day “dialing for dollars” rather than studying policy. The predictable result is a system where policy serves the donor class far more effectively than it serves the public.

Sortition destroys this incentive structure entirely. If legislative and executive positions are filled by random lottery from the adult citizen population, there are no campaigns, no fundraising, and no need to please wealthy patrons. A randomly selected nurse, welder, teacher, or small business owner would enter office without having made any promises to donors. They would owe nothing to anyone except the Constitution and their own conscience.

Critics claim that ordinary citizens would be “easily manipulated” by lobbyists. This is condescending nonsense. Professional politicians have spent decades mastering the art of appearing principled while selling out. Randomly selected citizens, chosen for a fixed term (say, three to six years), would bring fresh eyes and real-world experience. They could be supported by professional staff, expert panels, and mandatory transparency rules. More importantly, because no individual would serve long enough to build a career on influence-peddling, and because no one could run again, the incentive to sell favors for future campaign support evaporates. Sortition does not merely reduce corruption. It makes the current form of systemic corruption structurally impossible.

Sortition dramatically reduces pernicious partisanship and gridlock.

American politics has become a blood sport of negative partisanship. Primaries reward the most extreme candidates. General elections reward those who can best demonize the other side. The result is a Congress where the most powerful skill is not wisdom or compromise but tribal loyalty and rhetorical combat. Moderates and independent thinkers are systematically eliminated. The public correctly perceives both parties as captured by their respective bases and donor classes.

Sortition breaks this cycle by selecting representatives who reflect the actual distribution of the American public rather than the self-selected group of highly partisan political junkies willing to run for office. A truly random sample would include conservatives, liberals, libertarians, populists, and—crucially—millions of ordinary people who currently don’t vote because they find both parties repulsive. These citizens would not arrive in office with decades of partisan baggage or a need to signal tribal loyalty to win the next primary.

Evidence from citizens’ assemblies worldwide shows that randomly selected groups, when given time to deliberate with balanced information, tend to move toward practical, evidence-based solutions rather than ideological purity tests. They are far more willing to compromise because they lack the career incentives that reward intransigence. A Congress chosen by sortition would still contain disagreements—this is healthy—but it would be dramatically less likely to descend into the performative hatred and institutional paralysis that currently defines Washington.

Sortition genuinely empowers ordinary people—the true promise of democracy.

The most devastating indictment of the current system is how profoundly disconnected it is from the lived experience of average Americans. Most members of Congress are wealthy, highly educated, and have spent their adult lives inside the political-media bubble. They understand polling, fundraising, and television optics far better than they understand raising children on $45,000 a year, running a small business, or working night shifts in a hospital.

Sortition restores the radical idea that ordinary citizens are capable of governing themselves. It tells every American—not just the ambitious, the charismatic, or the wealthy—that they may be called upon to help steer the country. This is not merely symbolic. The psychological and cultural effects would be profound. Civic education would become urgently relevant because any citizen might actually need the knowledge. Political alienation would decrease because the government would literally be composed of people’s neighbors, coworkers, and family members rather than a permanent political class.

The claim that average citizens are too ignorant or irrational to govern is the eternal excuse of every ruling elite in history. Yet the same Americans who are supposedly too stupid to serve in Congress are trusted to run multi-million-dollar businesses, perform complex surgeries, fly commercial airliners, raise families, and serve on juries where they routinely make life-and-death decisions. The evidence is clear: when given clear information, adequate time, and proper structure, diverse groups of ordinary citizens consistently outperform professional politicians on complex policy questions.

Addressing the critics

Some will object that sortition removes “accountability” because officials cannot be voted out. But this misunderstands both accountability and the current system. Most incumbents win reelection due to name recognition, gerrymandering, and massive fundraising advantages. True accountability is nearly nonexistent. Sortition creates a different and more powerful form of accountability: the knowledge that one is a temporary steward of power, not its permanent owner, and that one’s decisions will be scrutinized by history and by fellow citizens who will soon return to private life.

Others worry about competence. This can be addressed through careful design: minimum eligibility requirements (age, citizenship, no serious criminal record), mandatory training periods, access to expert advisors, and the ability to remove officials through supermajority votes for cause. The executive could still include professional administrators while the top leadership positions are randomly selected. The details can be refined. The fundamental principle—that power should be distributed broadly among the citizenry rather than hoarded by a professional political class—must not be compromised.

Conclusion

The United States was founded on the revolutionary premise that people could govern themselves without kings or hereditary aristocrats. That experiment succeeded in many ways but eventually replicated the very problem it sought to escape: the emergence of a new ruling class whose interests diverge from those of the people. Elections, in a mass technological society, have become the mechanism by which this new class maintains and legitimizes its power.

Sortition offers a genuine reset. It removes the financial corruption that distorts policy. It reduces the partisan hatred that paralyzes government. Most importantly, it returns power to where it rightfully belongs—with ordinary American citizens. The nurse from Ohio, the truck driver from Texas, the software engineer from California, and the farmer from Iowa would have the same chance to shape the nation’s future as any career politician.

The choice is clear. We can continue pretending that tweaking campaign finance laws or shaming politicians will fix a system whose incentives are fundamentally rotten. Or we can embrace the radical but proven idea that democracy works best when it is literally rule by the people—chosen at random, serving temporarily, and returning to private life with their integrity and the republic intact.

The time for sortition has come. The American people are ready. The only question is whether we have the courage to trust ourselves again.
