Sortition: Arguments for Lottery-Based Governance

What Sortition Actually Means

Sortition involves selecting officeholders through random selection from eligible citizen pools, rather than competitive elections. It was practiced in ancient Athens and has contemporary advocates across the political spectrum. Understanding the arguments requires treating them seriously while maintaining analytical honesty about where they're genuinely compelling versus where they're speculative or contested.

The Core Arguments

1. Reducing Elite Capture

The argument: Elections systematically favor wealthy, well-connected, professionally polished candidates. Campaign finance requirements, name recognition advantages, and media dynamics create structural barriers that filter out ordinary citizens before voting even occurs.

Supporting evidence:

  • Congressional wealth substantially exceeds median household wealth
  • Incumbency advantages often exceed 90% in safe districts
  • Fundraising requirements effectively screen candidates by social network
  • Professional political consultants, donor relationships, and party infrastructure favor established elites

Where this is genuinely strong: The descriptive claim that elected legislatures are demographically unrepresentative is empirically well-supported. Sortition would likely produce bodies statistically closer to population demographics across income, education, occupation, and geography.

Honest complications: Wealth and connections don't explain everything about electoral outcomes. Voter preferences, ideological sorting, and genuine candidate quality also matter. The "elite capture" critique applies more powerfully to some systems (US Senate) than others (proportional representation parliaments).

2. Descriptive Representation

The argument: A randomly selected legislature would proportionally represent women, racial minorities, working-class people, rural communities, and other groups who are systematically underrepresented in elected bodies.

The statistical logic: With sufficient pool size and random selection, demographic representation becomes a matter of probability rather than political will. You don't need diversity programs, quota systems, or coalition negotiations—randomness achieves rough demographic parity automatically.

Contemporary examples cited:

  • Citizens' assemblies in Ireland (abortion, same-sex marriage)
  • British Columbia electoral reform assembly
  • French Citizens' Convention on Climate
  • Participatory budgeting panels in various cities

Where this is genuinely strong: These assemblies have produced thoughtful, nuanced deliberation on difficult topics, sometimes reaching consensus that elected bodies couldn't achieve. The Irish cases are particularly notable—randomly selected citizens resolved constitutional questions that professional politicians had gridlocked.

Honest complications:

  • Descriptive representation (looking like the population) doesn't automatically produce substantive representation (governing in the population's interest)
  • Small assembly sizes introduce significant sampling error
  • Selection bias still occurs if participation is voluntary

3. Reducing Partisan Polarization

The argument: Electoral incentives systematically reward extreme positions, base mobilization, and oppositional rhetoric. Politicians optimize for winning primaries and fundraising rather than governing well. Random selection eliminates these incentive structures entirely.

The mechanism: An elected politician must constantly calculate how positions affect reelection. A sortitioned official has no electoral future to protect, no donor class to satisfy, no party apparatus demanding loyalty. They can reason more freely about what's actually good policy.

Where this is genuinely strong: Primary election dynamics do demonstrably pull candidates toward ideological extremes. The "median voter" theorem breaks down when party base voters dominate primaries. This is a real structural problem sortition addresses directly.

Honest complications:

  • Accountability mechanisms exist for a reason—fear of losing reelection punishes genuinely bad performance
  • Removing electoral accountability doesn't eliminate political pressure; it just changes who applies it (lobbyists, administrators, peer groups)
  • Non-elected officials are not automatically more reasonable; they bring their own biases and are potentially more susceptible to capture by whoever provides information

4. Enhanced Deliberative Quality

The argument: When ordinary citizens are given time, resources, information, and structured deliberation, they reason well about complex policy questions. They approach problems without precommitment to partisan positions, respond to evidence more openly, and often find pragmatic common ground.

Research basis: Deliberative polling (James Fishkin's research) consistently shows that informed citizen panels shift toward more nuanced, evidence-responsive positions compared to baseline public opinion. People can handle complexity when given proper support.

Where this is genuinely strong: The evidence from deliberative mini-publics is fairly robust. Informed citizens do deliberate thoughtfully. This challenges assumptions that ordinary people can't engage with policy complexity.

Honest complications:

  • Deliberative polling involves careful facilitation, curated information, and small group dynamics that don't automatically scale to governance
  • Quality of deliberation depends heavily on information sources—sortitioned bodies are potentially very vulnerable to whoever controls the briefing materials
  • There's a difference between a temporary citizens' assembly advising on one question versus a permanent legislative body managing thousands of simultaneous complex issues

5. Eliminating Career Political Class Incentives

The argument: Professional politicians develop interests distinct from their constituents: maintaining power, building post-office career prospects, serving donors who fund future ambitions, building personal brands. Sortition eliminates career political incentives because there's no career to build.

Where this is genuinely strong: Revolving door dynamics between government and lobbying, post-office speaking fees, and campaign finance relationships do create real conflicts of interest that sortition would structurally eliminate.

Honest complications:

  • Short-term officeholders may be more vulnerable to capture by permanent bureaucracies and expert classes who provide continuity
  • Expertise accumulation matters for complex governance—the learning curve problem is real
  • "No career incentive" doesn't mean "no personal incentive"—ideology, social pressure, and immediate self-interest still operate

Structural Design Variations

Different sortition advocates propose different systems, which affects the strength of various arguments:

Design Element Options Trade-offs
Pool eligibility All adults vs. filtered criteria Inclusivity vs. competency concerns
Participation Mandatory vs. voluntary Representativeness vs. autonomy
Term length Short (1 year) vs. longer (4 years) Accountability vs. learning curve
Body size Small (150) vs. large (1000+) Deliberative quality vs. statistical representation
Combination Sortition only vs. hybrid with elections Radical change vs. incremental reform
Staff/expert role Advisory vs. directive Informed decisions vs. expert capture

Genuinely Strong Cases for Sortition

Being honest about where the arguments are most compelling:

Strongest applications:

  • Constitutional/fundamental questions where partisan gridlock prevents resolution
  • Oversight bodies checking elected officials
  • Deliberative supplements to elected legislatures
  • Local governance on specific bounded questions

The Irish model is the most empirically supported: a citizens' assembly with a bounded question, good facilitation, diverse information sources, and advisory (not binding) authority produced outcomes that resolved issues elected politicians couldn't touch.

Serious Objections That Advocates Must Address

The Expertise Problem

Complex modern governance involves trade law, monetary policy, military strategy, public health systems, and thousands of technical domains. Random selection doesn't produce expertise. Advocates respond that elected officials also lack expertise and rely on staff—but this means the real power shifts to permanent administrators, potentially reducing accountability without improving competence.

The Accountability Problem

Elections, for all their flaws, create a mechanism where poor performance has consequences. Removing this mechanism entirely raises the question: what prevents a sortitioned official from governing badly, lazily, or corruptly? Advocates propose recall mechanisms and evaluation systems, but these require their own enforcement institutions.

The Legitimacy Problem

Democratic legitimacy in modern understanding is substantially tied to consent expressed through voting. A government lottery winner who makes decisions affecting your life raises genuine questions about whether you've consented to their authority in any meaningful sense. This isn't merely traditionalism—it's a substantive question about the basis of political obligation.

The Information Vulnerability Problem

Whoever controls what information sortitioned officials receive has enormous influence. Elected officials develop independent information networks over time. New sortitioned officials are particularly dependent on bureaucratic staff and expert briefings, potentially concentrating power in exactly the permanent class sortition supposedly checks.

The Cohesion Problem

Legislatures need to form coalitions, maintain institutional memory, develop working relationships with executive agencies, and sustain policy over time. Randomly selected rotating bodies may struggle with organizational coherence in ways that impede effective governance.

Balanced Assessment

What sortition advocates are right about:

  • Electoral systems do systematically underrepresent ordinary people
  • Partisan incentives do distort policy in real ways
  • Citizen deliberation, when properly supported, does work better than cynics assume
  • Current democratic systems have serious structural problems worth fundamental reform

What the evidence actually supports:

  • Sortition works demonstrably well as a supplement to elections for specific deliberative purposes
  • Citizens' assemblies have genuine achievements on constitutional questions
  • Mixed systems (some elected, some sortitioned) have theoretical advantages over pure alternatives

What remains speculative:

  • That full legislative replacement would produce better outcomes than reformed electoral systems
  • That sortitioned officials would resist capture better than elected ones over time
  • That legitimacy problems would resolve through habituation rather than creating governance crises

What sortition advocates often understate:

  • The real competency and continuity challenges of rotating amateur governance
  • Information dependency on permanent bureaucratic structures
  • The ways accountability mechanisms serve genuine functions, not just elite interests

Conclusion

The sortition argument is strongest as a critique of existing electoral systems and as a design principle for specific deliberative bodies. The evidence from citizens' assemblies is genuinely impressive and suggests real democratic potential. The case for complete replacement of elections is considerably weaker—not because ordinary citizens can't govern thoughtfully, but because the structural problems of accountability, expertise, legitimacy, and information control don't disappear under sortition; they relocate to potentially less visible and less checkable locations.

The most intellectually honest position: sortition offers valuable tools for democratic reform, particularly in hybrid systems, and its strongest advocates are raising real problems with electoral democracy that deserve serious responses rather than dismissal.

A Speech for the Sortition Revolution

"Let Government Belong to the People Again"

The following is a persuasive advocacy speech presenting one position in a genuine democratic reform debate. I've tried to make it intellectually honest rather than a rhetorical trick.

My fellow citizens,

I want to ask you something uncomfortable.

When did you last feel like the government was yours?

Not theirs — not the donors', not the consultants', not the carefully managed candidates' — but yours. The government of a teacher in Cincinnati, a nurse in Phoenix, a mechanic in Birmingham, a farmer in Minnesota.

If you're struggling to remember, I think that tells us everything we need to know.

The System We Defend Is Broken By Design

We call what we have "democracy." But let's be honest about what it actually produces.

Congress has a consistent approval rating below 20 percent — yet re-election rates hover above 90 percent. Think about what that means. We hate the institution. We keep returning the same people. That isn't democracy. That is incumbency machinery.

The average winning Senate campaign now costs over $20 million. A House seat costs over $2 million. Before a single vote is cast, before a single constituent is heard, a candidate must become acceptable to people with extraordinary wealth. Every successful politician has already passed a donor primary that you never voted in.

Political scientists have a name for what we actually have. In a landmark 2014 study, Princeton researchers Gilens and Page analyzed 1,779 policy outcomes and found that economic elites and organized interest groups had substantial impact on policy, while average citizens had near-zero independent influence.

Near. Zero.

We have elections. We do not have democracy.

The Ancient Solution We Abandoned

Here is what most civics classes don't teach you:

The Athenians, who invented democracy, considered elections to be an oligarchic tool.

Aristotle said it plainly: elections favor the wealthy, the well-connected, the rhetorically skilled, the famous. Elections, he argued, produce aristocracy — rule by those considered superior — not democracy.

The Athenian solution was sortition: the random selection of citizens to serve in government, the same way we select juries today.

This wasn't a fringe idea. It was the core mechanism of Athenian democratic governance for nearly two centuries. And it worked remarkably well for a civilization that laid the intellectual foundations of Western thought.

We use this principle right now, today, in our own legal system. When your fate hangs in the balance, when life and liberty are at stake, we don't elect twelve jurors. We randomly select twelve of your peers — because we understand, intuitively, that selection eliminates the corrupting pressures of competition.

Why do we trust random citizens with questions of guilt and innocence — but not questions of taxation, healthcare, and foreign policy?

What Sortition Would Actually Look Like

I am not asking you to abandon structure. I am asking you to replace a broken selection mechanism with a fair one.

Imagine this:

A Citizens' Assembly of 535 people — stratified randomly to reflect the actual demographic composition of America. The right proportion of teachers and doctors and tradespeople and retirees. The right balance of rural and urban, young and old, the comfortable and the struggling. Selected the same way jurors are selected, with ability to excuse genuine hardships.

These citizens would serve defined terms — two to four years. They would receive full compensation comparable to their career earnings, so no one is punished financially for serving. They would have professional staff, policy experts, and research support — the same institutional knowledge currently available to elected members.

For the executive, we could implement a Citizens' Council — a small randomly selected body that appoints, oversees, and can recall executive leadership, much as citizens' assemblies in Ireland and Iceland have already demonstrated is workable.

This is not chaos. This is structured, supported civic service.

Why This Is More Democratic, Not Less

Let me address you directly if you're skeptical.

"Random people can't run a government."

Can they do worse than the people currently running it? We have $33 trillion in debt accumulated by credentialed professionals. We have a healthcare system that randomly selected farmers could hardly have designed to be more cruel and confusing. We have a tax code that a room of ordinary people would find genuinely embarrassing.

But more importantly — this objection proves too much. It's the same argument used against expanding the franchise to women, to non-property owners, to formerly enslaved people. "They're not ready. They're not qualified." It is, at its core, an aristocratic argument dressed in pragmatic clothing.

The research on citizens' assemblies — real ones, in Ireland, Canada, Iceland, France, Belgium — consistently shows that ordinary people, given information, time, and deliberative structure, make thoughtful, nuanced policy recommendations that frequently outperform what professional politicians produce. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly produced the framework for constitutional reforms on same-sex marriage and abortion that the political class had gridlocked for decades. They did it with integrity and depth.

Ordinary people can govern. They just haven't been given the chance.

The Anti-Corruption Argument Is Airtight

How do you bribe someone who hasn't been selected yet?

How do you run attack ads against a randomly selected citizen?

How do you build a thirty-year donor relationship with someone chosen by lottery?

You can't.

The corruption we live with isn't primarily the result of bad people. It is the structural consequence of competitive elections. When you must raise millions of dollars to win, you will go where the millions are. When you must win a primary, you will serve your primary voters more than your actual constituents. When your career depends on visibility, you will prioritize visibility over substance.

Sortition doesn't depend on the virtue of individuals. It removes the structural incentives for corruption. That is a far more durable solution than hoping we elect better people.

The Representation Argument Is Overwhelming

The 118th Congress is:

  • Over 90% college educated in a country where 38% hold degrees
  • Disproportionately wealthy — median net worth roughly 12 times the national median
  • Majority lawyers and businesspeople in a country where most people are neither
  • Significantly older than the population they represent
  • Still not reflective of the gender, racial, or class composition of America — despite progress

Sortition would produce a legislature that looks like America — not by engineering quotas, but by the mathematics of random selection across stratified categories. For the first time in American history, the people making laws about minimum wage would include people who have lived on minimum wage. The people making healthcare policy would include people who have worried about affording prescriptions. The people deciding on student loan policy would include people carrying student loans.

That is not just symbolism. Lived experience is a form of expertise that our current system systematically excludes.

Anticipated Objections, Honestly Addressed

I respect you too much to ignore the hard questions.

"This eliminates accountability — we can't vote them out."

This is a serious concern. My answer: sortition changes the accountability mechanism, it doesn't eliminate it. Citizens' assemblies can include recall provisions, performance reviews, and mandatory transparency. Moreover, consider what electoral accountability actually produces: politicians who are accountable to donors and base voters, not to the general public. Gilens and Page showed us that electoral accountability has already largely failed to produce policy accountability to ordinary citizens. We should debate what better accountability looks like — and I think term-limited, transparent service with citizen oversight boards is a serious answer.

"People won't want to serve."

Jury duty suggests otherwise — most citizens, when called, serve. Nations that have run citizens' assemblies find high acceptance rates when participation is properly supported and compensated. And sortition, unlike jury duty, comes with full pay, staff support, and genuine power. That changes the calculation.

"This is unconstitutional."

Yes — and so was ending slavery, until it wasn't. Constitutional amendment is the proper mechanism for fundamental reform, and Americans have done it twenty-seven times. This argument is about should we, not can we.

"Experts should make policy."

Experts should inform policy. They currently capture policy. There is a profound difference between a randomly selected assembly with access to the best policy expertise in the world, and allowing experts and their affiliated interest groups to effectively write the legislation. The first is democracy enhanced by expertise. The second is technocracy wearing a democratic costume.

The Deeper Argument: What Democracy Is For

I want to close with something more fundamental than mechanisms.

Reducing Partisanship

Sortition can also mitigate the hyper-partisanship that plagues American politics. Elections often devolve into tribalistic contests between political parties, leading to gridlock and divisive policymaking. Sortition, by contrast, creates a representative body that mirrors the diversity of the population, including political affiliations. This diversity fosters a more collaborative and deliberative decision-making process, reducing partisan entrenchment.

Furthermore, representatives chosen by lot would not owe their positions to political parties, freeing them from party discipline and allowing them to vote according to their conscience and the interests of their constituents.

Empowering Ordinary People

At the heart of sortition is the belief that ordinary people, given the opportunity and necessary support, can make effective political decisions. This is backed by numerous deliberative polling experiments and real-world applications like Ireland's Citizens' Assembly (Farrell et al., 2019).

Replacing elections with sortition offers a bold path forward for American democracy. By removing the scourge of political corruption, reducing partisanship, and empowering ordinary people, sortition can help restore trust in government and create a more responsive and representative political system.

The transition to sortition would be complex and require careful planning, including determining the selection process, term lengths, and training for representatives.     • Executive Lottery: Certain executive roles (e.g., heads of regulatory agencies) are filled by lottery.
  • Rotation in Office: Mandating a regular rotation of elected officials, coupled with a lottery system for those seeking re-election.

The Case for Sortition: Revitalizing American Democracy Through Random Citizen Selection

Introduction: The Democratic Paradox

At the heart of America’s founding lies a paradox: the very system designed to represent the people has become alienated from them. Elections, once hailed as the cornerstone of self-governance, now function as mechanisms of exclusion, corruption, and polarization. Money dominates campaigns, partisan gridslock stifles progress, and voter apathy reflects a deep disillusionment. What if there was a better way—a method that embodies equality, minimizes corruption, and reinvigorates civic engagement? The answer lies in sortition, the random selection of citizens to serve in legislative and executive roles. This ancient practice, used in Athenian democracy, offers a transformative path forward. By replacing elections with sortition, the United States could cleanse its political system of corruption, dissolve entrenched partisanship, and empower ordinary Americans in a truly representative democracy.

1. Eradicating Corruption: Severing the Tie Between Money and Power

Modern elections are, fundamentally, auctions. The cost of running for office has skyrocketed—a Senate race averages over $10 million, and presidential campaigns exceed billions. This financial barrier ensures that candidates are beholden to wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups. Once in office, politicians spend much of their time fundraising rather than governing. The result is a legalized form of corruption where policy is often shaped by who provides the money, not who provides the votes.

Sortition dismantles this system entirely. If leaders are chosen by lottery, campaign financing becomes irrelevant. There is no need to court donors, no super-PACs, no revolving doors between lobbying and legislature. A randomly selected citizen would enter office without prior debts or affiliations, focused solely on serving the public interest. Corruption—which thrives on access and influence—cannot take root in a system where access is guaranteed by chance, not cash. As political theorist Hélène Landemore notes, sortition “removes the distortionary effect of money from the political process,” allowing governance to return to its proper purpose: serving the people.

2. Dissolving Partisanship: From Ideological Warfare to Civic Duty

Elections in the United States have become exercises in tribal loyalty. The two-party system encourages polarization, as candidates appeal to base voters through extreme rhetoric and negative campaigning. Once elected, officials face intense pressure from their party to vote along ideological lines, often leading to gridlock and dysfunction. Compromise is framed as betrayal, and governance suffers.

Sortition breaks this cycle. Randomly selected citizens are not politicians by trade, nor are they bound by party discipline. They come from diverse backgrounds—farmers, teachers, engineers, artists—bringing lived experience rather than ideological scripts. Without partisan careers to protect, they are more likely to deliberate on issues based on evidence and communal interest rather than party dogma. Historical examples, such as Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly (which used sortition to address divisive issues like abortion and climate change), demonstrate that random samples of citizens can reach nuanced, bipartisan solutions. In a sortition-based legislature, debates would focus on problems, not posturing.

3. Empowering Ordinary People: True Representation Through Equality of Chance

Elections are an inefficient and exclusionary form of representation. They favor those with wealth, charisma, or existing networks—qualities not necessarily tied to wisdom or empathy. As a result, the political class is disproportionately drawn from professional politicians, lawyers, and business elites, detached from the everyday struggles of most Americans. Voter turnout hovers around 60%, with marginalized communities often underrepresented.

Sortition embodies the democratic principle of “one person, one chance.” Every eligible citizen has an equal probability of being selected, making the legislature a true microcosm of society. This approach ensures that the perspectives of ordinary workers, caregivers, and community members are directly included in decision-making. Moreover, because selection is random, citizens see themselves in their representatives—fostering trust and engagement. Research shows that citizens chosen by lot often take their role seriously, feeling a profound sense of duty to their communities. When people witness someone “like them” in a position of power, democracy ceases to be a spectator sport and becomes a shared enterprise.

4. Addressing Counterarguments: Competence, Accountability, and Stability

Critics raise concerns about sortition’s viability: Would random citizens be competent to govern? How would accountability work without elections? Would this lead to instability?

  • Competence: Modern governance does not require specialized expertise in lawmaking—most legislation is drafted by staff and experts. A diverse body of citizens, supported by nonpartisan advisors, brings a breadth of perspectives that often surpasses that of career politicians. Deliberation, not preexisting knowledge, is key. As historian Bernard Manin argues, sortition ensures “the rule of the ordinary” rather than “the rule of the expert.”
  • Accountability: Elections provide illusory accountability—voters rarely recall officials, and gerrymandering insulates incumbents. Sortition replaces electoral accountability with immediate transparency: selected citizens serve limited terms, return to their communities, and are subject to direct peer review. Their decisions must be publicly justified, fostering a culture of reasoned justification.
  • Stability: Sortition systems can include safeguards—such as expert advisory panels, review periods, and consensus requirements—to ensure thoughtful continuity. Long-term policies (e.g., infrastructure, climate) would benefit from insulation against short-term electoral cycles.

5. A Historical and Global Perspective

Sortition is not utopian fantasy; it has deep historical roots and modern applications. Athenian democracy used lotteries to select most officials, believing randomness ensured freedom from faction. Today, citizens’ assemblies—randomly selected groups that deliberate on public issues—have been used effectively in Canada, Australia, and the European Union to tackle polarizing topics with surprising success. In the United States, experiments with “deliberative polling” show that informed, randomly selected citizens often arrive at wiser policy positions than the general public or elected officials.

Adopting sortition at the national level would be a natural evolution of these practices, extending the principle of civic lottery from advisory roles to governing institutions.

Elections were designed for a different era—an era without mass media, digital manipulation, and vast inequality. Today, they perpetuate corruption, polarization, and exclusion. Sortition offers a radical yet pragmatic alternative: a system where leadership is drawn by chance, where money loses its grip, and where every citizen—not just the privileged few—has a real chance to shape the nation’s future.

By embracing sortition, the United States could rediscover the essence of democracy: not the rule of the few, but the participation of the many. It would be a bold step, but one rooted in ancient wisdom and modern evidence. In the words of political scientist Robert Dahl, “The ideal of democracy is that all citizens should have an equal chance of being heard and of influencing decisions.” Sortition makes that ideal a reality. It is time to trust chance—and in so doing, to trust each other.

Sortition: The Case for Randomly Selected Government

The idea of sortition — selecting political leaders by lottery rather than election — is one of democracy's oldest concepts. Ancient Athens used it extensively for its citizen assemblies, and it's experienced a serious intellectual revival in recent decades among political theorists like Hélène Landemore, Alexander Guerrero, and others. Here's the strongest case proponents make:

1. The Electoral Problem It Claims to Solve

Traditional elections, according to sortition advocates, produce systematic distortions rather than genuine representation:

  • Selection bias toward the privileged: Campaigns require enormous money, social networks, media access, and personal time. This filters for people who already possess wealth, fame, or institutional backing — exactly the opposite of the general population.
  • Elite capture: Once in office, elected officials become dependent on donors, party structures, and interest groups for reelection, creating predictable patterns of policy influence.
  • The "selection illusion": Voters often choose from a menu they didn't create. Primaries are controlled by parties; general elections by name recognition and funding. The set of available candidates is itself a form of selection before voters ever participate.
  • Rational ignorance: In large electorates, individual votes have negligible impact. This rationally discourages deep engagement with policy substance, shifting attention to personality, branding, and emotional appeals.

Sortition advocates argue these aren't bugs to be patched — they're structural features of electoralism that cannot be fixed within the election framework itself.

2. The Case for Sortition's Benefits

Radical Fairness and Statistical Representation

If you randomly selected 100 people from a country, they would — with remarkable statistical regularity — mirror the population's diversity in age, gender, race, income, education, geography, occupation, and ideology. Elections approximate this; sortition achieves it mathematically.

A sortition assembly would naturally include:

  • Working-class people, not just those who can afford to campaign
  • Individuals with disabilities, rural residents, immigrants — groups chronically underrepresented in elected bodies
  • People with no political ambition whatsoever, who might bring different priorities

The argument: democracy means rule by the people, and the most literal interpretation is that the government should look like the people — not like people who want power.

Reduction of Elite and Institutional Control

Campaign finance, lobbying, media gatekeeping, and party machinery all serve as filters that concentrate power among organized, well-resourced groups. Sortition bypasses these mechanisms entirely. You cannot "lobby" a lottery. You cannot buy influence over a process that selects people who have no pre-existing political debts or ambitions.

This is perhaps the most compelling argument for proponents: sortition eliminates the pipeline through which concentrated wealth and institutional power translate into concentrated political power.

Fresh Perspective and Reduced Groupthink

Long-serving elected officials and career politicians develop habits of thought, institutional loyalties, and risk-aversion patterns. Sortition would periodically inject people who think about problems in fundamentally different ways — teachers, plumbers, artists, single parents — who approach policy from lived experience rather than political training.

Research on citizens' assemblies (small-scale sortition bodies used in Ireland, France, Canada, and elsewhere) consistently shows that randomly selected citizens, when given good information and structured deliberation, reach thoughtful, often surprising policy conclusions that differ from those of professional politicians.

Elimination of the "Perpetual Campaign"

Modern elected officials spend enormous portions of their time fundraising and managing public image rather than governing. Sortition removes this distortion entirely. Selected citizens serve their term and return to private life, with no reelection strategy to distort their priorities.

Reduced Polarization

Electoral politics incentivizes conflict, tribal identity, and performative opposition — these are tools for winning votes. Sortition assemblies, composed of people with no party affiliation and no reelection concerns, have shown in practice a greater capacity for deliberation, compromise, and evidence-based reasoning.

3. How It Might Work in Practice

Proponents don't typically advocate for pure randomness with no structure. Common proposals include:

  • Stratified random sampling: Ensuring the lottery draws proportionally from demographic categories so the assembly statistically mirrors the population
  • Citizens' assemblies as a complement: Randomly selected bodies that deliberate on specific issues (like Ireland's assemblies on abortion and marriage equality) alongside or constraining elected bodies
  • Full legislative sortition: A chamber entirely composed of randomly selected citizens serving fixed terms (e.g., 2-5 years), perhaps paired with an elected chamber
  • Mandatory participation with opt-out: Treating civic service like jury duty, with the right to decline but a civic expectation to serve if selected
  • Support infrastructure: Providing selected citizens with stipends, childcare, education on issues, and structured deliberation support

4. Legitimate Concerns Critics Raise

To be fair, sortition advocates must grapple with serious objections:

  • Competence: Legislating and governing require specialized knowledge. Randomly selected citizens may lack expertise in economics, law, or international affairs. Proponents respond: elected officials rarely have these competencies either, and experts can advise any body.
  • Accountability: If leaders are random, who do you hold responsible for bad outcomes? Proponents argue accountability through elections is largely illusory anyway.
  • Legitimacy and consent: People may not accept the authority of leaders they didn't choose. Proponents note that Athenians accepted sortition as more democratic than elections, and citizens' assemblies have high public trust.
  • Vulnerability to manipulation: A sortition body could still be influenced by media, experts, or institutional pressures. This is a real concern, though proponents argue the lack of pre-existing political incentives mitigates it.
  • Scalability: Citizens' assemblies have worked for specific issues in specific countries. Scaling to full national governance is untested.

5. The Deeper Philosophical Question

At its core, sortition challenges a fundamental assumption embedded in modern democracy: that choosing leaders is the democratic act.

Sortition advocates argue the truly democratic acts are:

  • Drawing leaders from the people (randomness achieves this perfectly)
  • Deliberating together about common problems (which can be structured)
  • Holding power accountable through transparency and rotation (not through the charade of elections)

They suggest that elections were a compromise invented for large, complex states that lacked the tools for direct participation — and that modern communication and deliberation infrastructure might make that compromise unnecessary.

This is genuinely one of the most interesting open questions in democratic theory. The evidence from citizens' assemblies is surprisingly encouraging, and the philosophical challenges to electoralism are substantive. Whether sortition represents the future of governance or an interesting intellectual exercise remains to be seen — but the conversation it provokes already reveals deep assumptions about what democracy is actually for.
